summary: STARx Viewer is a free web tool that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared all-sky survey into something anyone can explore. Type any sky coordinates, a target name, or open a shared link, and within seconds you see that patch of sky as a “blink” animation across every SPHEREx survey pass, the same technique that found Pluto. Objects that move, like nearby brown dwarfs or a possible Planet X, jump between frames, while a difference image and a deep coadd make faint changes visible. Every star known to ESA’s Gaia mission is marked at its position on each date, so anything moving that Gaia does not know stands out. Users can read the real spectrum and light curve of any pixel across 0.75–5 µm, check SPHEREx quality flags, and report candidates to a shared database that every later visitor sees. The backend keeps up with new SPHEREx data automatically, so the tool grows with the survey and helps citizen scientists take part in the search for new worlds.
details:
What it does
STARx Viewer lets anyone watch the infrared sky change over time with NASA SPHEREx data. The user enters RA/Dec (degrees or sexagesimal), picks one of the five challenge targets, or opens a URL with coordinates, and chooses a field of view from 1 to 20 arcminutes. The tool shows:

  • a blink animation of all SPHEREx epochs, per detector (D1–D6) or all six combined for higher signal-to-noise;
  • a difference image (last minus first), a “compare two dates” mode and a deep coadd of all epochs;
  • every ESA Gaia DR3 star in the field, moved with its proper motion to each frame’s date. Point sources without a Gaia counterpart are highlighted as possible new objects;
  • the spectrum (0.75–5 µm, using the real wavelength of every pixel) and the light curve of any clicked pixel, coloured by epoch;
  • pixel values under the cursor: surface brightness, zodiacal light, signal-to-noise, wavelength, and decoded SPHEREx quality flags, plus the share of flagged pixels per frame;
  • a “Report a candidate” button. Reports go to a shared database, appear as markers for every later visitor, show how many people reported the same spot, and warn when the spot is a known target.

How it works
A Python FastAPI backend on Google Cloud Run searches NASA/IPAC IRSA for every SPHEREx image covering the position. It then reads only the needed pixels directly from the official SPHEREx copy on Amazon S3 (AWS Open Data), up to 32 files in parallel. In our tests this took 10–20 s instead of 90–136 s, and the data is identical to IRSA’s. The science module subtracts zodiacal light, groups images into survey epochs, stacks them per detector using the SPHEREx Level 2 flags, and produces the frames, difference images, coadds, spectra and light curves. A quick one-image-per-epoch preview appears first, and results are cached in Google Cloud Storage. The backend checks IRSA daily for new observations and rebuilds results automatically, and new data releases need only a configuration change. The five challenge targets are bundled precomputed, so they always open instantly, even if the archive is down. Gaia stars come from VizieR with mirror fallback and are cached permanently. The React/TypeScript frontend is hosted on Vercel.

Benefits and impact
Moving-object searches are well suited to human eyes: volunteers have found many of the known brown dwarfs by blinking images. STARx Viewer makes SPHEREx data blink-ready for anyone without downloading gigabytes or writing code. The Gaia overlay, the quality flags and the shared candidate database help separate real discoveries from known stars and artefacts. The open API and URL links let other projects embed the tool.

Tools and languages
Python (FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery, reproject, photutils, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Pillow, s3fs/fsspec), TypeScript, React, Vite, Docker, GitHub Actions, Google Cloud Run, Google Cloud Storage, Vercel, Amazon S3 (AWS Open Data).

Use of Artificial Intelligence
Yes. The team used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant: to understand the challenge and SPHEREx data, plan the work split and API, write and review parts of the backend, science and frontend code, find IRSA documentation, and help with deployment and these texts. We ran and checked all results ourselves: we verified that the S3 data is identical to IRSA’s, measured the speed, and confirmed that Barnard’s Star moves north by about 10″ per year in our images. AI-assisted source files are marked in their headers. No AI-generated images, video or audio are presented as NASA data.
